To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
financial risk tolerance, income adequacy and the influence of social norms are significant predictors of financial efficacy towards long-term saving behaviour.
The results of this study suggest that financial efficacy and savings behaviour are positively related.
financial risk tolerance, social norms and perceived income adequacy are significant predictors of desirable savings behaviour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theoretical model for the enhancement of retirement savings amongst low-income consumers in East London, South Africa.

the identification of rational and irrational indicators of financial efficacy and desirable savings behaviour among low-income consumers in order to promote financial security during the pre-retiree phase of life.
the development of an effective and efficient savings behaviour intervention strategy, with the ultimate aim of increasing the retirement savings rate of low-income consumers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
financial advisors can use the findings to increase financial needs awareness amongst their clients.

financial efficacy, as a composite indicator, is significantly associated with long-term savings behaviour, whilst financial risk tolerance is the strongest predictor of long-term savings behaviour amongst low-income consumers.
this study has provided a better understanding of the financial efficacy of low-income consumers and the influence of such determinants on savings behaviour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
financial efficacy and selfreported savings behaviour are not only influenced by rational factors, but also by irrational ones.

this study provides an empirical foundation for the development of a more holistic approach to financial education in order to promote the long-term financial security and well-being of low-income consumers.
the findings of this study can assist in improving low-income consumers’ retirement savings behaviour, which in turn can contribute to the alleviation of poverty in South Africa.
The main takeaway from our work is that

financial advisors can use the results of this study to develop a better understanding of the financial needs of low-income consumers, which may be applied to develop more targeted financial education programmes.
low-income consumers are not as financially illiterate as previously thought and that their savings behaviours are not solely driven by rational factors.
financial advisors need to focus on improving the financial literacy of low-income consumers, and to assist in developing a positive attitude towards savings.
